questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of reading `a[i]` from an array of $n$ elements, given a valid index $i$?
questions.explanation: Array elements occupy contiguous storage of equal width, so the address of element $i$ is computed arithmetically as $\text{base} + i \times \text{width}$. That is one multiplication, one addition and one memory read regardless of $n$, so access is constant time. This random-access property is the defining advantage of contiguous storage.

distractorRationale.b: $O(\log n)$ is the cost of *searching* a sorted array by bisection, not of indexing it
distractorRationale.c: $O(n)$ is the cost of traversing the array or of indexing a linked list
distractorRationale.d: $O(n \log n)$ is a sorting bound and does not arise from a single access

questions.stem: A zero-indexed array of 4-byte integers begins at address 2000. What is the address of element `a[7]`? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: The address is $\text{base} + i \times \text{width} = 2000 + 7 \times 4 = 2028$. The index is multiplied by the element width, not added to the base, and because indexing is zero-based no adjustment term is needed. If the array were one-indexed the formula would be $\text{base} + (i - 1) \times \text{width}$.

questions.stem: An array holds $n$ elements in a buffer with spare capacity. A new element must be inserted at index 0, preserving the order of the rest. What is the worst-case cost?

options.text: $O(\log n)$, by bisecting to find the insertion point
$O(n)$, because all $n$ existing elements must shift one position right

questions.explanation: Contiguity is the constraint. To free index 0 while keeping the sequence in order, every existing element must move one slot to the right, which is $n$ element moves. Spare capacity avoids a reallocation but does not avoid the shifting. Insertion at the *end* is the only position that is $O(1)$, which is why an array is a poor list but an excellent stack.

distractorRationale.a: Confuses having room in the buffer with having room at the front; capacity removes the reallocation, not the shift
distractorRationale.b: The insertion point is given as index 0, so no search is needed; bisection would not reduce the movement cost anyway
distractorRationale.d: Each shift is a single element move, so the total is $n$ moves, not $n$ operations of cost $n$

questions.stem: Appending to a doubling dynamic array is described as **amortised** $O(1)$. What does that claim mean?

options.text: Every individual append runs in constant time
Any sequence of $m$ appends costs $O(m)$ in total, so the average cost per append is constant even though some single appends cost $O(n)$
Appending is constant time on average over random inputs, but could be $O(n)$ on adversarial input
Appending is constant time only when the array's capacity is a power of two

questions.explanation: Amortised analysis bounds the total cost of a *sequence* of operations and divides by the sequence length. A resize does cost $\Theta(n)$, but doubling makes resizes exponentially rare, so the copying performed across $m$ appends totals fewer than $2m$ element moves. Note that this is a worst-case guarantee over the sequence, not a probabilistic one — no assumption about input distribution is involved.

distractorRationale.a: That is worst-case $O(1)$ per operation, a strictly stronger claim that a doubling array does not satisfy
distractorRationale.c: That describes *expected* time under a distributional assumption; amortisation makes no such assumption
distractorRationale.d: Powers of two are an implementation convenience; any constant growth factor greater than 1 gives the same amortised bound

questions.stem: A dynamic array grows by adding a **fixed 10 slots** each time it fills, instead of doubling. What is the total cost of $n$ appends?
questions.explanation: With a fixed increment there are about $n/10$ reallocations, and the $k$-th copies roughly $10k$ elements. The total is $\sum_{k=1}^{n/10} 10k = 10 \cdot \frac{(n/10)(n/10+1)}{2} = \Theta(n^2)$, giving amortised $\Theta(n)$ per append. Geometric growth is what makes the resize count logarithmic and the copy total linear; arithmetic growth destroys the guarantee no matter how large the constant increment.

distractorRationale.a: The constant increment makes each individual resize cheap in a sense, but the *number* of resizes becomes linear in $n$, so the costs compound
distractorRationale.b: $\Theta(n \log n)$ would arise if each of $\log n$ resizes cost $\Theta(n)$; here the resize count is linear, not logarithmic
distractorRationale.d: $\Theta(n\sqrt{n})$ is the total for growth by a $\sqrt{n}$-sized increment, not a fixed one

questions.stem: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles whenever an append finds it full. How many reallocations occur while appending 17 elements one at a time? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: The capacity sequence is 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, so a reallocation is triggered by the 2nd, 3rd, 5th, 9th and 17th appends — five in all. In general appending $n$ elements from capacity 1 causes $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ reallocations, and $\lceil \log_2 17 \rceil = 5$. Because the count grows only logarithmically, the copied elements total under $2n$.

questions.stem: Searching an **unsorted** array of $n$ elements for a given value requires $\Theta(n)$ comparisons in the worst case.
questions.explanation: True. With no ordering to exploit, any correct algorithm must be prepared to examine every element: if it skipped one, an adversary could place the target there. So the worst case is $n$ comparisons, and it is also the cost of concluding that the value is absent. Sortedness is exactly the precondition that allows bisection to reduce this to $\Theta(\log n)$.

questions.stem: Two implementations store one million integers and traverse them sequentially, summing every value. Both perform $\Theta(n)$ work, yet the array version is measured several times faster than the linked list version. What is the principal reason?

options.text: The array version performs asymptotically fewer operations
Contiguous storage gives spatial locality, so each cache line fetched supplies many consecutive elements, whereas list nodes are scattered and each visit risks a cache miss
Arrays are stored in registers rather than in main memory

questions.explanation: Both traversals are $\Theta(n)$; the difference is the constant factor, which asymptotic notation deliberately hides. A 64-byte cache line holds sixteen 4-byte integers, so an array traversal incurs roughly one miss per sixteen elements and benefits from hardware prefetching. List nodes are separately allocated, so each `next` dereference may miss, and the pointer field also inflates memory traffic. This is why $\Theta$ classes rank algorithms but do not predict wall-clock time.

distractorRationale.a: The operation counts are the same order; the gap is in cost per operation, not count
distractorRationale.c: Traversing a linked list once visits each node once, which is $\Theta(n)$
distractorRationale.d: A million integers cannot fit in the register file; both live in memory
